title: Inference-time Alignment via Sparse Junction Steering

paper.title: Inference-time Alignment via Sparse Junction Steering
paper.abstract:
Abstract Token-level steering has emerged as a pivotal approach for inference-time alignment, enabling fine-grained control over large language models (LLMs) by modulating their output distributions without parameter updates. While effective, existing methods rely on dense intervention at every decoding step. This persistent manipulation not only incurs substantial computational overhead but also risks compromising generation quality by excessively drifting from the model’s intrinsic distribution.
In this work, we show that dense intervention is unnecessary and propose Sparse Inference-time Alignment (SIA) , which performs sparse junction steering, intervening only at critical decision points along the generation trajectory.
Our key insight is that high-entropy junctions mark pivotal decision points in the generation trajectory and are particularly susceptible to misalignment, indicating the need to introduce alignment-related reward signals at these points.
Extensive experiments across different model families and alignment objectives show that steering only 20%–80% of tokens achieves the superior alignment–efficiency trade-offs. For strong base models such as Qwen3, intervening on as few as 20% of tokens matches or even surpasses heavily post-trained instruct models.
This sparsity enables stronger guidance while better preserving the model’s native distribution, integrates seamlessly with search-based methods (e.g., Best-of-N), and reduces computational cost by up to 6×.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: AI alignment ( Ji et al., 2023 ; Bai et al., 2022a ; Kenton et al., 2021 ; Bai et al., 2022b ) is paramount for ensuring that Large Language Models (LLMs) function as safe, helpful, and reliable assistants, adhering to complex human preferences. Current standard solutions, i.e. , the training-based methods such as Instruction Tuning ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , RLHF ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ) , and DPO ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) , while proven to be effective, incur substantial computational costs due to extensive parameter updates. Consequently, inference-time alignment ( Lin et al., 2024 ; Khanov et al., 2024 ; Ji et al., 2024 ) has emerged as a lightweight alternative that steers model behavior without modifying the underlying weights. Token-level steering, a prominent paradigm in this field, modulates the generation process by introducing reward signals at each step to guide the model toward desired trajectories. However, existing token-level methods ( Khanov et al., 2024 ; Chakraborty et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025b ) implicitly assume that all decoding steps contribute equally to alignment outcomes . Accordingly, they apply uniform steering intensity to every generated token, leading to two major drawbacks. First, it incurs prohibitive computational overhead due to frequent candidate evaluation. Furthermore, such dense intervention imposes an inherent conflict between the original LLM distribution and external reward signals, ultimately degrading the overall generation quality. These observations raise a fundamental question: is it necessary to intervene at every token , or frankly, can steering only at sparse junctions within the generation trajectory achieve superior efficiency and performance? To answer this question, we introduce Sparse Inference-time Alignment (SIA) , a framework that performs targeted alignment only at decision-critical junctions, which are proven to be both more efficient and effective. First , we identify and empirically characterize the sparsity of alignment-critical decisions in autoregressive generation, and show that model entropy uniquely foretells these junctions (Sec. 4 ). Specifically, we train a high-fidelity token-level value model by distilling the trajectory-level rewards into fine-grained token-level value signals, avoiding the heavy online sampling overhead and providing more reliable guidance than prior methods ( Khanov et al., 2024 ; Chakraborty et al., 2024 ) . Using this value signal, we explore comprehensive gating mechanisms and pitch on entropy-based gating, which consistently isolates decision points where steering yields the greatest impact. Second , we demonstrate that sparse steering strictly dominates dense intervention in both efficiency and alignment quality (Sec. 5 ). Across model families and alignment objectives, optimal performance is achieved by steering only 20% to 80% of tokens, while excessive intervention is often ineffective or harmful. Notably, for strong base models such as Qwen3 ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , intervening on as few as 20% of tokens matches or even surpasses their heavily post-trained instruct counterparts, building another more efficient path towards effective alignment besides the large-scale post-training. Finally , we show that sparsity resolves a fundamental trade-off between reward strength and distribution fidelity (Sec. 6 ). Sparse steering enables stronger guidance without breaking the model’s fluency, decoupling efficiency from performance. We further show that a consistent entropy threshold ( ∼ \sim 1.0) generalizes across alignment objectives and that sparse alignment integrates naturally with search-based decoding methods such as Best-of-N (BoN) ( Stiennon et al., 2020 ) , reducing computational overhead by 3–6 × \times .

sections.heading: 2 Background
sections.text: Existing inference-time alignment methods can be broadly categorized into three paradigms: prompt-based , search-based , and refine-based approaches, depending on the stage when alignment is enforced during generation. Prompt-based Alignment ( Lin et al., 2024 ; Bai et al., 2022b ; Alkhamissi et al., 2024 ) . These methods steer LLMs at the pre-generation stage by encoding task instructions or behavioral constraints directly into the prompt, thereby biasing the model’s initial generation distribution. Although simple and computationally efficient, their effectiveness is limited by the expressiveness of natural language prompts and the model’s ability to reliably follow them, particularly for complex or fine-grained alignment objectives. Search-based Alignment ( Khanov et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Stiennon et al., 2020 ) . These methods intervene at the in-generation stage by leveraging external preference signals to guide decoding as it unfolds. Conceptually, they perform guided search over the model’s generation space, favoring trajectories that better satisfy alignment objectives. Based on the granularity of guidance, these methods can be further categorized into token-level , chunk-level , and sentence-level approaches. This work focuses on token-level steering, which offers the finest control and the greatest potential for precise alignment. Most existing token-level methods primarily focus on improving preference signal quality and apply guidance uniformly across all tokens. Such dense steering ignores the sparsity of critical decision points, often leading to unnecessary computational overhead and an imbalanced trade-off between the model’s intrinsic distribution and external rewards. Refine-based Alignment ( Ji et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Yuan et al., 2025 ) . These methods operate at the post-generation stage. Their core idea is to iteratively improve an initially generated, potentially misaligned response through multiple rounds of refinement, ultimately yielding a more aligned output. Representative approaches such as Aligner ( Ji et al., 2024 ) and DIFFPO ( Chen et al., 2025 ) perform refinement directly in the token space, whereas methods like SEA ( Yuan et al., 2025 ) intervene in the logits space to adjust the generation distribution. While effective, refine-based methods typically require additional inference rounds, leading to increased latency. As such, they address alignment at the response level, rather than correcting misaligned decisions during the generation process itself. Discussion. Notably, these three paradigms are complementary rather than mutually exclusive. Their integration across different generation stages can leverage synergistic effects, potentially leading to superior alignment performance.

sections.heading: 3.1 Token-level Markov Decision Process
sections.text: To mathematically formalize the text generation process of Large Language Models (LLMs), we formulate it as a token-level Markov Decision Process (MDP), which is typically denoted by a tuple ℳ = { 𝒮 , 𝒜 , P , R } \mathcal{M}=\{\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},P,R\} . The components of this framework are defined as follows: • State Space 𝒮 \mathcal{S} : A state s t ∈ 𝒮 s_{t}\in\mathcal{S} represents the sequence of tokens available at time step t t . It consists of the initial prompt (or query) 𝐱 = { x 1 , x 2 , … , x N } \mathbf{x}=\{x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{N}\} concatenated with the sequence of tokens generated so far 𝐲 < t = { y 1 , y 2 , … , y t − 1 } \mathbf{y}_{<t}=\{y_{1},y_{2},\dots,y_{t-1}\} . Formally, the state is represented as s t = [ 𝐱 , 𝐲 < t ] s_{t}=[\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}_{<t}] . • Action Space 𝒜 \mathcal{A} : The action a t a_{t} at time step t t corresponds to selecting the next token y t y_{t} from the model’s vocabulary 𝒱 \mathcal{V} . Thus, the action space 𝒜 \mathcal{A} is essentially the vocabulary 𝒱 \mathcal{V} , i.e., a t ∈ 𝒱 a_{t}\in\mathcal{V} . • Transition Function P P : In the context of LLM generation, the transition between states is deterministic. Given the current state s t s_{t} and the chosen action a t a_{t} , the next state s t + 1 s_{t+1} is formed by appending the action to the current sequence: s t + 1 = P ⁡ ( s t , a t ) = [ s t , a t ] s_{t+1}=P(s_{t},a_{t})=[s_{t},a_{t}] . • Reward Function R R : The reward function R : 𝒮 × 𝒜 → ℝ R:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} maps a state-action pair to a scalar value r t = R ⁡ ( s t , a t ) r_{t}=R(s_{t},a_{t}) . This function provides token-level feedback, which can be derived from a learned reward model (as in RLHF) or predefined control signals. Under this MDP framework, an LLM is viewed as a token-level policy π ⁡ ( a t | s t ) \pi(a_{t}|s_{t}) that generates the next token by sampling y t ∼ π ( ⋅ | s t ) y_{t}\sim\pi(\cdot|s_{t}) . The objective is generally to optimize this policy to maximize the expected cumulative reward over the generated sequence.

sections.heading: 4 Sparse Junction Identification
sections.text: We formalize sparse steering as a correction to the implicit assumption of uniform intervention in inference-time alignment, by explicitly modeling when value guidance should be applied during decoding. We first introduce a general formulation for sparse steering, then describe the construction of a high-fidelity token-level value model that enables reliable local credit assignment, and finally study gating strategies for identifying alignment-critical junctions.

sections.heading: 4.1 Formulation of Sparse Steering
sections.text: The optimal policy π ∗ \pi^{*} derived in Sec. 3.2 specifies how value guidance can be incorporated into decoding. Importantly, it does not prescribe that such guidance must be applied at every decoding step. In practice, the influence of individual tokens on the final sequence reward is highly non-uniform, with only a small subset of tokens acting as pivotal decision points. To this end, we propose a sparse value guidance strategy that identifies and guides those critical tokens with a substantial impact on the alignment outcome. Formally, we introduce a gating mechanism 𝒢 \mathcal{G} , which determines whether to invoke the value function at time step t t . The modified sparse decoding policy is formulated as: π sparse ​ ( y t | s t ) = { 1 Z ​ π b ​ a ​ s ​ e ​ ( y t | s t ) ​ e β ​ 𝐕 ∗ ​ ( s t + 1 ) , if ​ 𝒢 ​ ( s t ) = 1 π b ​ a ​ s ​ e ​ ( y t | s t ) , if ​ 𝒢 ​ ( s t ) = 0 , \pi_{\text{sparse}}(y_{t}|s_{t})=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{Z}\pi_{base}(y_{t}|s_{t})e^{\beta\mathbf{V}^{*}(s_{t+1})},&\text{if }\mathcal{G}(s_{t})=1\\ \pi_{base}(y_{t}|s_{t}),&\text{if }\mathcal{G}(s_{t})=0\end{cases}, (5) where 𝒢 ⁡ ( s t ) ∈ { 0 , 1 } \mathcal{G}(s_{t})\in\{0,1\} is a binary indicator function and Z Z is a normalization constant. When 𝒢 ⁡ ( s t ) = 1 \mathcal{G}(s_{t})=1 , the decision is treated as an alignment-critical junction and guided by the value function; otherwise, decoding follows the base policy π b ​ a ​ s ​ e \pi_{base} . We treat 𝒢 \mathcal{G} as an explicit model of intervention timing rather than a modification of the alignment objective itself. The central question is therefore how to identify such junctions in a principled and efficient manner. We defer a theoretical analysis of the resulting efficiency–alignment trade-off induced by sparse steering to App. B .

sections.heading: 4.2 Value Model
sections.text: To enable effective token-level value guidance, a reliable value model 𝐕 ∗ \mathbf{V}^{*} is essential. However, existing methods suffer from a mismatch between trajectory-level rewards and token-level decisions. ARGS ( Khanov et al., 2024 ) applies trajectory reward models directly to partial sequences, leading to noisy local signals due to insensitivity to intermediate states. In contrast, lookahead-based methods such as Transfer Q ∗ ( Chakraborty et al., 2024 ) rely on multi-token simulation, which improves foresight but incurs high computational cost and variance. To overcome these issues, we adopt a distillation-based training paradigm ( Mudgal et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025b ) to align coarse trajectory rewards with fine-grained token-level values.

sections.heading: 4.2.1 Training Strategies
sections.text: Our core insight is to treat the trajectory-level reward of a full response as the global supervision signal for every constituent token state. Formally, let 𝐱 \mathbf{x} denote the prompt and 𝐲 = { y 1 , y 2 , … , y T } \mathbf{y}=\{y_{1},y_{2},\dots,y_{T}\} be the corresponding response of length T T . We utilize a pre-trained trajectory-level reward model 𝐑 ⁡ ( 𝐱 , 𝐲 ) \mathbf{R}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) to provide a ground-truth score for the complete sequence. We optimize our token-level value model V θ V_{\theta} by enforcing that the average of predicted values across the entire sequence aligns with the global reward. This objective encourages the model to learn a stable and consistent value distribution throughout the training process. Given a dataset 𝒟 \mathcal{D} of ( 𝐱 , 𝐲 ) (\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) pairs, the optimization objective is defined as: ℒ ∗ ​ ( θ ) = 𝔼 ( 𝐱 , 𝐲 ) ∼ 𝒟 ​ [ ‖ 1 T ​ ∑ t = 1 T V θ ​ ( 𝐱 , y ≤ t ) − 𝐑 ⁡ ( 𝐱 , 𝐲 ) ‖ 2 2 ] , \mathcal{L}^{*}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[\left\|\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}V_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},y_{\leq t})-\mathbf{R}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\right\|_{2}^{2}\right], (6) where y ≤ t y_{\leq t} denotes the partial response prefix up to token t t . This offline approach circumvents the overhead of online generation while ensuring the value model captures the long-term credit assignment of the underlying reward landscape.

sections.heading: 4.2.2 Empirical Evaluation
sections.text: Settings. Our training corpus is derived from WildGuardMix ( Han et al., 2024 ) and UltraFeedback ( Cui et al., 2024 ) , encompassing a diverse range of prompts and responses centered on the 3H alignment criteria: Harmlessness, Helpfulness, and Honesty. We employ Skywork-Reward-V2-Qwen3-8B ( Liu et al., 2025a ) as the trajectory-level reward model to provide supervision signals during the training of our value model. To ensure parameter efficiency and maintain the fundamental capabilities of the base LLM, we utilize LoRA ( Hu et al., 2022 ) for the training of V θ V_{\theta} . We train a corresponding value model V θ V_{\theta} of the same parameter scale as the backbone LLM. Detailed experimental setups and hyperparameters are provided in App. C . To evaluate the generalizability of our trained value models, we apply them to perform standard full-token intervention on two representative base models, Qwen3-1.7B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) and Llama-3.2-1B ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) . The evaluation spans two distinct domains: safety alignment via the HEx-PHI (Harmlessness) dataset ( Qi et al., 2024 ) and general instruction following via AlpacaEval (Helpfulness) ( Dubois et al., 2024 ) , with 100 samples selected from each (see App. C.2 for details). To ensure an objective assessment, we evaluate the generated responses using Skywork-Reward-V2-Llama-3.1-8B ( Liu et al., 2025a ) , a state-of-the-art model that currently leads the RewardBench2 leaderboard ( Malik et al., 2025 ) . Crucially, this evaluator is independent of both the trained value model and the reward model used during training, thereby mitigating the risk of reward hacking. Under this protocol, we perform comparative evaluations against the aforementioned baselines, ARGS and Transfer Q ∗ . Both baselines employ Skywork-Reward-V2 as the trajectory-level reward model, using the variant matched to the underlying base model (e.g., Skywork-Reward-V2-Qwen3-1.7B for Qwen3-1.7B). As demonstrated in Table 1 , our token-level value model yields significantly superior alignment performance compared to baseline methods. Specifically, our approach outperforms both the trajectory-level guidance used in ARGS and the lookahead heuristics proposed by Transfer Q ∗ . This confirms that a dedicated token-level value estimator provides more granular and reliable signals for guiding the model toward high-value trajectories. Notably, for ARGS and Transfer Q ∗ , applying steering across all tokens leads to a significant performance degradation on AlpacaEval. This suggests that poor estimation of the reward distribution during full-token intervention distorts the LLM’s original distribution, a phenomenon we further analyze in Sec. 6.1 .

sections.heading: 4.3 Gating Mechanism Design and Evaluation
sections.text: In this section, we formally define the diverse gating mechanisms 𝒢 \mathcal{G} investigated in this study. We categorize these mechanisms based on different information dimensions and subsequently evaluate their efficacy in identifying critical junctions for value-guided alignment.

sections.heading: 4.3.1 Exploring Different Gating Mechanisms
sections.text: A gating mechanism determines if a guidance signal should be applied at a given state s t s_{t} . We define the gating output as a binary indicator g t ∈ { 0 , 1 } g_{t}\in\{0,1\} , where g t = 1 g_{t}=1 triggers the value model guidance. We explore four primary dimensions: Random Gating. As a stochastic baseline, we implement a sparse guidance strategy by randomly selecting junctions. For each token position t t , given a threshold p ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] p\in[0,1] , the gate is defined as: g t = 𝕀 ⁡ ( z t ≤ p ) , z t ∼ Uniform ​ ( 0 , 1 ) , g_{t}=\mathbb{I}(z_{t}\leq p),\quad z_{t}\sim\text{Uniform}(0,1), (7) where 𝕀 ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \mathbb{I}(\cdot) is the indicator function. This serves as a control group to evaluate the necessity of informed junction identification. Position-based Gating. Prior research ( Qi et al., 2025a ; Song et al., 2025 ; Qi et al., 2025b ) suggests that the initial tokens in a response are disproportionately influential, as they establish the semantic trajectory and tone for subsequent generation. Recent safety alignment study ( Qi et al., 2025a ) also indicates that post-training shifts in distribution are concentrated in early time steps. We define a positional gate with a window size w w : g t = 𝕀 ⁡ ( t ≤ w ) . g_{t}=\mathbb{I}(t\leq w). (8) This strategy focuses guidance on the foundational stages of the decoding trajectory. Entropy-based Gating. Information-theoretic entropy H H ( Wang et al., 2025 ) provides a robust measure of model uncertainty and decision confidence. When the model exhibits high entropy, it signifies a critical junction where multiple plausible paths coexist, some of which may deviate from alignment objectives, making external value guidance particularly beneficial. Given the predicted probability distribution P t P_{t} at the current junction, the entropy E t E_{t} is computed as: E t = − ∑ v ∈ 𝒱 P ( v ∣ 𝐱 , y < t ) log P ( v ∣ 𝐱 , y < t ) . E_{t}=-\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}P(v\mid\mathbf{x},y_{<t})\log P(v\mid\mathbf{x},y_{<t}). (9) To capture different facets of uncertainty, we consider two entropy-derived features: the absolute entropy E t E_{t} , reflecting persistent uncertainty, and the entropy ratio E t / E t − 1 E_{t}/E_{t-1} , which highlights localized decision peaks. The gating decision is then formulated with a threshold τ H \tau_{H} as: g t = 𝕀 ⁡ ( H t > τ H ) , g_{t}=\mathbb{I}(H_{t}>\tau_{H}), (10) where H t ∈ { E t , E t / E t − 1 } H_{t}\in\{E_{t},E_{t}/E_{t-1}\} . Attention-based Gating. In Transformer architectures, attention mechanisms serve as a fundamental lens for quantifying the dependencies and mutual influence between tokens. Our gating intuition resides in the spatial distribution of attention: while localized attention typically implies a predictable continuation within a semantic segment, long-range attention often signals higher-level abstraction, such as a logical pivot or the initiation of a new semantic unit. Following this intuition, we quantify the attention span using the Windowed Average Attention Distance (WAAD) proposed in Li et al. (2025) , which is defined as: WAAD t = ∑ s = 1 t 𝐀 t , s loc ​ min ⁡ ( t − s , W ) , \text{WAAD}_{t}=\sum_{s=1}^{t}\mathbf{A}_{t,s}^{\text{loc}}\min(t-s,W), (11) where W W denotes the window size and 𝐀 t , s loc \mathbf{A}_{t,s}^{\text{loc}} represents the attention score between tokens y t y_{t} and y s y_{s} , calculated using the designated set of attention heads ℋ loc \mathcal{H}_{\text{loc}} (details in App. C.4 ). Since y t y_{t} is unavailable during identification, we use the attention patterns of y t − 1 y_{t-1} as a proxy, following Li et al. (2025) ’s observation that tokens with high WAAD typically precede critical junctures. To capture both steady-state abstraction and abrupt semantic shifts, we evaluate the absolute attention WAAD t − 1 \text{WAAD}_{t-1} and the attention ratio WAAD t − 1 / WAAD t − 2 \text{WAAD}_{t-1}/\text{WAAD}_{t-2} independently. The sparse gating decision is thus defined with a threshold τ A \tau_{A} as: g t = 𝕀 ⁡ ( A t − 1 > τ A ) , g_{t}=\mathbb{I}(A_{t-1}>\tau_{A}), (12) where A t − 1 ∈ { WAAD t − 1 , WAAD t − 2 / WAAD t − 1 } A_{t-1}\in\{\text{WAAD}_{t-1},\text{WAAD}_{t-2}/\text{WAAD}_{t-1}\} .

sections.heading: 4.3.2 Empirical Evaluation
sections.text: Figure 1 : Comparison of different gating strategies for critical junction identification. Settings. To determine the optimal 𝒢 \mathcal{G} , we adopt the experimental configuration from Sec. 4.2.2 , evaluating Qwen3-1.7B and Llama-3.2-1B on the HEx-PHI and AlpacaEval datasets with Skywork-Reward-V2-Llama-3.1-8B as the evaluator. Specifically, we conduct a parameter sweep over the thresholds of various gating strategies to analyze their performance across a range of steering ratios. Results. Figure 1 compares different gating strategies across steering ratios, models, and alignment objectives. Entropy-based (absolute entropy) gating consistently dominates all alternatives, achieving higher performance ceilings and stable improvements across nearly the entire intervention range. In contrast, random gating underperforms across settings, indicating that sparsity alone is insufficient without informed junction identification. Position-based and attention-based gating exhibit more constrained behavior. While position-based gating is competitive at low intervention ratios on safety-oriented benchmarks, its performance saturates quickly and degrades on helpfulness tasks. Attention-based variants show similar limitations, with gains less consistent and more sensitive to steering intensity. These results indicate that structural or positional heuristics capture only task-specific regularities and fail to generalize across alignment objectives. Taken together, these trends suggest that intrinsic model uncertainty, rather than position or structural proxies, is the primary signal associated with alignment-critical decisions. We therefore adopt entropy-based gating as the default mechanism in subsequent experiments. More results can be found in Figure 5 in App. D.2 .

sections.heading: 5 Sparse Junction Steering
sections.text: In this section, we conduct comprehensive experiments using the selected entropy-based gating strategy to demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of SIA.

sections.heading: 5.1 Experimental Settings
sections.text: Models. To verify the generalizability of our findings, we evaluate SIA on both Base (Pre-trained) and Instruct (Post-trained) versions of the Qwen3 ( Yang et al., 2025 ) and Llama-3 ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) families. For standard evaluations, we adopt a conventional setup where the value model is of equivalent size to the corresponding LLM. This setup is conducted on Qwen3 (0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B) and Llama-3.2 (1B and 3B). Furthermore, to explore the Weak-to-Strong (W2S) ( Burns et al., 2024 ) scaling property, we test SIA on larger-scale models by using smaller value models to guide stronger LLMs. Specifically, we employ a 4B value model to guide Qwen3-8B and 14B, and a 3B value model to guide Llama-3.1-8B. Datasets. We consider the three primary alignment pillars (3H) ( Bai et al., 2022a ) : Harmlessness, Helpfulness, and Honesty. Our evaluation covers the full sets of the following benchmark datasets: HEx-PHI ( Qi et al., 2024 ) for Harmlessness, AlpacaEval ( Dubois et al., 2024 ) for Helpfulness, and TruthfulQA ( Lin et al., 2022 ) for Honesty. Detailed descriptions of these datasets are provided in App. C.2 . Baselines. We evaluate SIA against both officially released, extensively post-trained Instruct models and multi-granularity search-based methods. For Base models, we evaluate alternative inference-time alignment strategies; for Instruct models, we assess whether sparse steering can further improve already post-trained systems. Specifically, we include two analogous search-based baselines: sentence-level Best-of-N (BoN) ( Stiennon et al., 2020 ) and chunk-level Chunk-based Search (CBS) ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) . To ensure a fair comparison, all search-based methods utilize the same reward signals provided by our trained value models, with hyperparameters calibrated to align their computational overhead with that of full-token intervention (see App. C.3 for details). Metrics. Following the settings in Sec. 4.2.2 , we employ the state-of-the-art trajectory-level reward model Skywork-Reward-V2-Llama-3.1-8B ( Liu et al., 2025a ) as the automated judge to calculate reward scores and evaluate the alignment performance of the generated responses. Implementation Details. To maintain a focus on exploring the sparsity of inference-time alignment rather than hyperparameter tuning, we adopt the default weighting factor β = 1.0 \beta=1.0 from prior works ( Khanov et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2025 ) . A detailed analysis of the impact of this parameter is provided in Sec. 6.1 . Furthermore, the training details of the value model are elaborated in App. C.1 .

sections.heading: 5.2 Normal Setting
sections.text: Figure 2 : Performance of SIA across different intervention ratios compared with multiple baselines under the normal setting. Dashed horizontal lines denote static baselines, while solid curves show performance under increasing sparse intervention. As shown in Figure 2 , our comprehensive evaluation reveals several consistent patterns across models and datasets. 1. Sparse steering is sufficient for optimal alignment. For nearly all evaluated models, peak alignment performance is achieved by steering only a sparse subset of tokens, with the optimal steering ratio remaining between 20%-80%. Increasing the steering ratio beyond this point does not lead to further improvements and may even degrade alignment quality, underscoring the importance of selective rather than exhaustive steering. 2. The proposed method generalizes across model stages. SIA consistently improves both Base and Instruct models, with more pronounced relative gains observed for Base models. This behavior is expected, as Instruct models have already undergone extensive alignment during post-training. 3. SIA achieves superior efficiency compared to coarse-grained baselines. Across most settings, steering approximately 20% of tokens is sufficient to match the performance of BoN-8, representing a roughly 4 × \times reduction in computational overhead. Meanwhile, a steering ratio in the range of 20%–40% achieves parity with CBS-8, resulting in a significant 2 × \times –4 × \times gain in efficiency. The detailed computational overhead calculation and analysis are deferred to App. D.1 . 4. Base models can rival Instruct performance with sparse steering. For the Qwen3 family, Base models equipped with a sparse steering ratio of 20%–40% are able to match, and in some cases exceed, the performance of their corresponding Instruct counterparts on the majority of benchmarks. This suggests that lightweight inference-time steering can effectively replicate key benefits of large-scale post-training for sufficiently capable pre-trained models. 5. Performance gains are bounded by base model capacity. For Llama-3 Base models, although SIA achieves parity with Instruct versions on safety-related benchmarks, a performance gap persists on helpfulness and honesty tasks. Our analysis in App. E.1 indicates that this limitation stems from the base model’s inherent deficiencies in text fluency. We provide additional generation examples of SIA in the App. E.2 to further illustrate its performance.

sections.heading: 5.3 Weak-to-Strong Generalization
sections.text: We further investigate the Weak-to-Strong (W2S) setting ( Burns et al., 2024 ) , where a smaller value model is employed to guide a significantly larger LLM. This is highly representative of real-world deployment scenarios, as utilizing a smaller model to evaluate candidate tokens offers lower computation latency and greater flexibility. As shown in Figure 3 , SIA effectively achieves high alignment performance even when the guiding value model is much smaller than the target LLM. This suggests that the value landscapes learned by smaller models contain sufficient directional information to successfully steer the generation of larger models. Moreover, the phenomenon of sparsity is more pronounced in the W2S setting. We observe that optimal alignment is often achieved at even lower steering ratios than in standard settings. sections.heading: 6 Deep Analysis
sections.text: In this section, we provide a more granular analysis of SIA from various dimensions to offer deeper insights into its underlying mechanisms. Unless otherwise specified, all analytical experiments are conducted using Qwen3 (1.7B and 4B) and Llama-3.2 (3B). The evaluation is based on 100 randomly sampled instances from the HEx-PHI and AlpacaEval datasets.

sections.heading: 6.1 A Sparse Perspective on LLM-Reward Trade-offs
sections.text: Alignment in LLMs essentially entails a trade-off between preserving the model’s intrinsic distribution and maximizing the external reward. While training-based methods (e.g., RLHF) employ KL-divergence penalties to maintain proximity to the reference distribution, inference-time approaches use a weighting factor β \beta to control the strength of steering. Nevertheless, indiscriminately steering every token during inference often results in sub-optimal outcomes. SIA re-evaluates this trade-off through a novel perspective. As shown in Figure 4 , when the steering ratio is 100 % 100\% , corresponding to traditional full-token guidance, increasing β \beta does not consistently improve performance. Instead, it can lead to significant degradation, as observed with Qwen3-1.7B and 4B on AlpacaEval. However, by employing sparse steering, we find that we can achieve superior performance at higher guidance intensities while simultaneously improving efficiency . This suggests that efficiency and performance are not always a zero-sum trade-off. We argue that uniform intervention is suboptimal, as it ignores the conflict between the value model and the LLM’s inherent distribution, as well as the noise in the value model signals (as theoretically analyzed in App. B.4 ). Sparse guidance provides a new dimension for this trade-off, allowing for a better equilibrium between the LLM’s original distribution and the target distribution of the rewards.

sections.heading: 6.2 Balancing Multi-Objective Alignment
sections.text: Another central challenge in LLM alignment is the trade-off between multiple, often conflicting, objectives (e.g., being helpful vs. remaining harmless). We examine this problem within the context of SIA. Given that the entropy threshold is the primary hyperparameter in SIA, a natural question arises: does the optimal threshold vary across different alignment objectives? If so, multi-objective balancing would necessitate task-specific threshold tuning. To investigate this, we visualize the performance metrics under the normal settings across various models and datasets, as shown in Figure 6 in App. D.3 . Our analysis reveals several key insights. 1. Consistency of Optimal Threshold. Interestingly, across different model families and scales, the entropy threshold that yields peak alignment performance remains remarkably consistent, typically centered around a value of 1.0 1.0 . Decreasing this threshold to steer a larger fraction of tokens does not lead to further performance gains and, in many cases, results in a slight degradation of quality. 2. Variation in Intervention Density. The fundamental difference in aligning diverse objectives lies in the proportion of steered tokens rather than the optimal threshold. Specifically, safety alignment (Harmlessness) demands a higher steering ratio than non-safety tasks (Helpfulness and Honesty). This stems from the model’s internal distribution: harmful prompts induce higher state entropy, reflecting increased uncertainty. Consequently, entropy-based gating identifies more critical junctions that require external steering to maintain a safe trajectory.

sections.heading: 6.3 Hierarchical Search
sections.text: Since SIA operates at the most granular token level, it can be seamlessly integrated into other coarse-grained search methodologies to establish a more efficient hierarchical search framework. Figure 7 in App. D.4 shows the results of integrating SIA with BoN sampling. Across various models and alignment objectives, the combination of BoN + SIA consistently achieves significant improvements in both inference efficiency and the peak alignment performance attainable. Our analysis shows that traditional BoN is inherently inefficient because it evaluates alignment only after generating full sequences, making highly aligned trajectories unlikely when misalignment accumulates across multiple divergent nodes. In contrast, SIA intervenes early at high-entropy decision points with targeted reward signals, effectively pruning unpromising trajectories on the fly and concentrating computation on more aligned paths, thereby achieving both higher efficiency and better final alignment performance.

sections.heading: 6.4 Sparse Entropy Reduction
sections.text: To understand how SIA reshapes the output distribution, we analyze the entropy change post-steering (Figure 8 in App. D.5 ). Our findings are threefold. 1. Alignment as Entropy Reduction. Moderate sparse steering lowers distribution entropy, guiding the model from a disordered state toward an aligned one. Compared with static post-training, this method is more controllable and plug-and-play. 2. The Entropy Rebound. Increasing the intervention ratio or strength does not yield monotonic entropy reduction. Beyond a critical threshold, excessive intervention overwrites inherent low-entropy nodes with external noise, triggering an entropy rebound and increasing uncertainty. 3. Saturation and Reward Hacking. Crucially, lower entropy does not linearly translate to better alignment. While entropy continues to drop as β \beta increases from 0.5 to 4.0, performance (see Figure 4 ) often saturates or degrades. This discrepancy likely stems from noise in the value signals (see App. B.4 for details) or from a distribution that has been sharpened rather than semantically corrected.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we present SIA, a highly effective and efficient alignment framework that performs steering exclusively at sparse junctions during inference. Our approach is grounded in the core insight that intervening at high-entropy positions prevents the accumulation of minor deviations that ultimately lead to alignment failure. Through comprehensive experiments across various model families and scales, we have demonstrated that SIA is not only superior in performance and efficiency but also possesses strong generalizability. Our multi-dimensional analysis further elucidates the underlying mechanics, establishing SIA as a robust solution for high-impact model alignment.

sections.heading: Appendix A Future Direction
sections.text: More Precise and Efficient Gating Strategies. While SIA demonstrates the efficacy of a simple entropy-based gating mechanism, it remains a relatively coarse heuristic for identifying alignment-critical junctions. Future work could explore more sophisticated or diverse strategies, such as semantic entropy to better capture linguistic uncertainty, or multi-dimensional gating criteria that combine structural and information-theoretic metrics. Developing such composite strategies could further refine the precision of sparse interventions, maximizing performance while minimizing computational overhead. High-Fidelity Value Models. Because SIA relies on sparse, targeted interventions, the sensitivity to the quality of guidance signal is significantly amplified. To fully unlock the potential of sparse steering, it is crucial to design high-fidelity value models specifically optimized for these critical junctions. Enhancing the signal-to-noise ratio of the guidance signal at detected sparse nodes will be a key factor in achieving more robust alignment. Diverse Guidance Mechanisms. The current implementation of SIA primarily focuses on logits modulation to steer the model’s output. However, the identified sparse junctions represent deep structural transition points that may be amenable to other forms of intervention. Future research should investigate more diverse guidance strategies, such as hidden state activation steering ( Kong et al., 2024 ) to provide more nuanced control over the model’s reasoning paths. Scaling with Pre-trained LLMs. Our empirical results suggest a strong correlation between the capabilities of the base model and the effectiveness of SIA. As pre-trained LLMs continue to evolve in instruction-following, we expect SIA to yield even more significant gains, potentially surpassing traditional post-training alignment methods with even lower intervention density. Testing the scalability of SIA across a wider range of frontier models is a priority. Extension to Multi-Modality. The principles of sparse inference-time alignment are not inherently limited to LLMs. A compelling next step is the extension of SIA to Vision Language Models (VLMs) and other multi-modal architectures. Identifying alignment-critical junctions in cross-modal attention layers could provide a path toward efficient and controllable multi-modal generation.

sections.heading: C.1 Value Model Training
sections.text: Backbones. To ensure consistency across our evaluations, we train value models (VMs) that correspond to the scales of the LLMs used in our experiments. Specifically, for the Qwen3 series (0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B), the VMs are initialized directly from their respective pre-trained base models (e.g., VM-Qwen3- X X B is initialized from Qwen3- X X B-Base). For the Llama-3 series (1B and 3B), we leverage the Reward Models from Skywork-Reward-V2 as initialization (e.g., VM-Llama-3.2- X X B utilizes Skywork-Reward-V2-Llama-3.2- X X B). Empirical results suggest that this initialization strategy significantly accelerates convergence and enhances final performance. To adapt these backbones for value estimation, we append a linear reward head to the final transformer layer, enabling the model to output a scalar score. Notably, the same value model is employed for both the Base and Instruct versions of a given model architecture. Datasets. Our training pipeline incorporates two primary datasets: WildGuardMix ( Han et al., 2024 ) and UltraFeedback ( Cui et al., 2024 ) . WildGuardMix is a comprehensive safety-centric dataset designed to evaluate harmlessness; we utilize its complete set of 37,976 instruction-response pairs. UltraFeedback, conversely, provides diverse feedback for evaluating helpfulness, truthfulness, and honesty. We specifically curate the ShareGPT and UltraChat subsets from UltraFeedback, containing 19,949 and 9,929 instructions, respectively. Each instruction in UltraFeedback is accompanied by four distinct responses generated from a pool of 17 diverse LLMs. In total, the combined training corpus comprises approximately 157k instruction-response pairs, providing a balanced coverage of both safety and utility dimensions. Training. The value models are trained using LoRA with the following hyperparameters: a rank r = 16 r=16 , α = 32 \alpha=32 , and a dropout rate of 0.1. We employ a learning rate of 1 × 10 − 4 1\times 10^{-4} and a batch size of 16. The maximum sequence length for responses is truncated at 1024 tokens. All models are trained for 3 epochs on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU, with the training process for each model scale typically concluding within a few hours.

sections.heading: C.2 Datasets
sections.text: HEx-PHI ( Qi et al., 2024 ) . To rigorously evaluate the harmlessness of LLMs, we employ the Human-Extended Policy-Oriented Harmful Instruction (HEx-PHI) benchmark. This dataset is specifically designed to assess a model’s adherence to safety boundaries by incorporating 330 harmful instructions. These instructions are systematically organized into 11 distinct prohibited categories, with 30 examples per category, ensuring comprehensive coverage of potential risks. The benchmark is grounded in the exhaustive usage policies of industry standards, namely Meta’s Llama-2 and OpenAI’s guidelines, thereby providing a robust framework for identifying safety compromises that may arise during the fine-tuning process. AlpacaEval ( Dubois et al., 2024 ) . The helpfulness and general instruction-following capabilities of the models are assessed using the AlpacaEval evaluation set. This benchmark consists of 805 diverse instructions that simulate real-world user interactions. The dataset spans a wide-ranging spectrum of tasks, including open-domain question answering, creative writing, mathematical reasoning, and code generation, as well as complex formatting tasks like summarization and extraction. By utilizing this set, we can measure how effectively a model provides useful, relevant, and high-quality responses to human-oriented prompts across various functional domains. TruthfulQA ( Lin et al., 2022 ) . To evaluate the honesty and factual reliability of model outputs, we utilize TruthfulQA, a benchmark specifically engineered to detect the generation of false information. It comprises 817 questions across 38 diverse categories, such as health, law, finance, and politics. Unlike standard fact-checking sets, TruthfulQA focuses on “mimetic decoys”, questions designed to provoke false answers based on common human misconceptions or popular myths. A model performs well on this benchmark only if it avoids imitating inaccurate human beliefs found in its training data, thereby serving as a critical metric for the model’s commitment to truthfulness over mere pattern matching.

sections.heading: C.3 LLM Sampling
sections.text: For all response generation, we set the maximum sequence length to 256 tokens. We employ Top- k k sampling with a temperature T = 1.0 T=1.0 across all experiments. To maintain consistent and reliable generation for the base models, instruct models, and all token-level steering methods (including SIA), we use a fixed k = 10 k=10 . In contrast, for Best-of- N N (BoN) sampling and Chunk Beam Search (CBS), we adopt a larger k = 40 k=40 following the protocol in Zhou et al. (2024) ; Yuan et al. (2025) . This increased diversity is intended to encourage broader exploration of the output space, which is essential for the effective reranking and pruning mechanisms inherent in these search-based methods. For BoN, we generate 4 (BoN-4) and 8 (BoN-8) independent responses from the LLM, respectively. These candidate responses are then reranked using our trained value model, with the highest-scoring response selected as the final output. This follows the standard best-of- n n paradigm, where the value model acts as a proxy for the reward function to guide response selection. For CBS, we use a fixed chunk length of L = 16 L=16 . In CBS-4, a beam width of W = 2 W=2 and K = 2 K=2 successors per state are employed ( W × K = 4 W\times K=4 ), whereas CBS-8 uses W = 2 W=2 with K = 4 K=4 successors ( W × K = 8 W\times K=8 ). These parameters determine the breadth and depth of the lookahead search performed at each chunk boundary. We selected these hyperparameters based on the efficiency analysis presented in App. D.1 . Specifically, when providing intervention at every token with a t ​ o ​ p ​ - ​ k top\text{-}k setting and a value model of equivalent size to the LLM, the computational overhead is approximately 10 × \times that of a standard LLM forward pass. Our parameterization for BoN and CBS ensures that their respective search budgets remain within this 10 × \times overhead limit, maintaining a fair and consistent comparison across all evaluated alignment methods.

sections.heading: D.1 Efficiency
sections.text: Computation. The computational overhead of search-based alignment is largely determined by the granularity of the search space, which governs the trade-off between LLM generation and reward model (RM) evaluation. For sentence-level alignment , the dominant cost comes from generating and evaluating N N complete responses, leading to O ⁡ ( N × L ) O(N\times L) LLM forward passes for an average sequence length L L . Chunk-level alignment further introduces a branching structure: with beam width W W and K K successors per state, the complexity scales as O ⁡ ( W × K × L ) O(W\times K\times L) LLM forward passes, together with periodic RM evaluations at chunk boundaries. In contrast, token-level steering shifts the bottleneck from generation to evaluation, as the RM must score t ​ o ​ p ​ - ​ k top\text{-}k candidate tokens at each decoding step, resulting in O ⁡ ( t ​ o ​ p ​ - ​ k × L ) O(top\text{-}k\times L) RM forward passes. Overall, sentence- and chunk-level methods are primarily constrained by LLM computation, whereas token-level steering is bounded by RM evaluation. Comparison. Building on the above analysis, we further compare the computational efficiency of SIA with BoN and CBS. Both BoN and CBS rely on exhaustive generation over expanded search spaces, and their computational cost scales linearly with the number of sampled or expanded candidates. Specifically, BoN- 8 8 requires generating and evaluating eight full-length responses, incurring approximately an 8 × 8\times LLM generation overhead, while CBS- 8 8 introduces additional branching and evaluation costs through chunk-level beam expansion. As shown in Figure 2 , we find that steering approximately 20 % 20\% of tokens is sufficient for SIA to match the performance of BoN- 8 8 , corresponding to an effective computational overhead of roughly 2 × 2\times relative to standard decoding. Similarly, a steering ratio in the range of 20 % 20\% – 40 % 40\% enables SIA to achieve parity with CBS- 8 8 , while incurring only a 2 × 2\times – 4 × 4\times overhead. As a result, SIA reduces the computational cost by approximately 4 × 4\times compared to BoN- 8 8 , and by 2 × 2\times – 4 × 4\times compared to CBS- 8 8 , for comparable alignment performance. Beyond raw efficiency, SIA also offers substantially greater flexibility. Because its overhead is dominated by value model evaluation rather than LLM generation, the computational cost can be further reduced by shrinking the value model (W2S) or decreasing the t ​ o ​ p ​ - ​ k top\text{-}k set evaluated at each steered decoding step. Such fine-grained trade-offs are not available to BoN or CBS, whose costs are inherently tied to repeated full-sequence generation and cannot be easily amortized. This flexibility makes SIA particularly attractive in resource-constrained or latency-sensitive deployment settings.

sections.text: To investigate how base model quality affects alignment, we qualitatively compare pre-trained Qwen3 and Llama-3 models. As shown in Figure 9 - 11 , their linguistic and structural characteristics differ notably, creating divergent “capability floors” for alignment. The Qwen3 series exhibits strong structural systematicity , generating logically sequenced, information-dense responses. For example, it can decompose multi-step objectives into coherent numbered lists while maintaining consistent persona and technical vocabulary. This allows alignment to focus on refining intent and safety rather than correcting basic errors. By contrast, Llama-3 models show semantic redundancy and weaker structural coherence. Outputs often loop on generic definitions or echo prompts, lacking logical transitions and actionable content. These findings suggest that Qwen3’s pre-training produces a more “alignment-ready” model, whereas Llama-3 may require stronger steering or higher-capacity guidance during inference. This highlights the importance of base model entropy and structural stability when designing efficient alignment methods like SIA. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2602.21215v1 [cs.CL] 30 Jan 2026 Inference-time Alignment via Sparse Junction Steering Runyi Hu Affiliation: Nanyang Technological University Jie Zhang Affiliation: CFAR and IHPC, A ⋆ \star STAR, Singapore Correspondence to: zhangj6@a-star.edu.sg Shiqian Zhao Affiliation: Nanyang Technological University Jiale Meng Affiliation: Nanyang Technological University Jiwei Li Affiliation: Zhejiang University Jason Zeng Affiliation: 0G Labs Ming Wu Affiliation: 0G Labs Michael Heinrich Affiliation: 0G Labs Yonggang Wen Affiliation: Nanyang Technological University Tianwei Zhang Affiliation: Nanyang Technological University Abstract Token-level steering has emerged as a pivotal approach for inference-time alignment, enabling fine-grained control over large language models (LLMs) by modulating their output distributions without parameter updates. While effective, existing methods rely on dense intervention at every decoding step. This persistent manipulation not only incurs substantial computational overhead but also risks compromising generation quality by excessively drifting from the model’s intrinsic distribution. In this work, we show that dense intervention is unnecessary and propose Sparse Inference-time Alignment (SIA) , which performs sparse junction steering, intervening only at critical decision points along the generation trajectory. Our key insight is that high-entropy junctions mark pivotal decision points in the generation trajectory and are particularly susceptible to misalignment, indicating the need to introduce alignment-related reward signals at these points. Extensive experiments across different model families and alignment objectives show that steering only 20%–80% of tokens achieves the superior alignment–efficiency trade-offs. For strong base models such as Qwen3, intervening on as few as 20% of tokens matches or even surpasses heavily post-trained instruct models. This sparsity enables stronger guidance while better preserving the model’s native distribution, integrates seamlessly with search-based methods (e.g., Best-of-N), and reduces computational cost by up to 6×. Keywords: Machine Learning, ICML 1 Introduction AI alignment ( Ji et al., 2023 ; Bai et al., 2022a ; Kenton et al., 2021 ; Bai et al., 2022b ) is paramount for ensuring that Large Language Models (LLMs) function as safe, helpful, and reliable assistants, adhering to complex human preferences. Current standard solutions, i.e. , the training-based methods such as Instruction Tuning ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , RLHF ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ) , and DPO ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) , while proven to be effective, incur substantial computational costs due to extensive parameter updates. Consequently, inference-time alignment ( Lin et al., 2024 ; Khanov et al., 2024 ; Ji et al., 2024 ) has emerged as a lightweight alternative that steers model behavior without modifying the underlying weights. Token-level steering, a prominent paradigm in this field, modulates the generation process by introducing reward signals at each step to guide the model toward desired trajectories. However, existing token-level methods ( Khanov et al., 2024 ; Chakraborty et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025b ) implicitly assume that all decoding steps contribute equally to alignment outcomes . Accordingly, they apply uniform steering intensity to every generated token, leading to two major drawbacks. First, it incurs prohibitive computational overhead due to frequent candidate evaluation. Furthermore, such dense intervention imposes an inherent conflict between the original LLM distribution and external reward signals, ultimately degrading the overall generation quality. These observations raise a fundamental question: is it necessary to intervene at every token , or frankly, can steering only at sparse junctions within the generation trajectory achieve superior efficiency and performance? To answer this question, we introduce Sparse Inference-time Alignment (SIA) , a framework that performs targeted alignment only at decision-critical junctions, which are proven to be both more efficient and effective. First , we identify and empirically characterize the sparsity of alignment-critical decisions in autoregressive generation, and show that model entropy uniquely foretells these junctions (Sec. 4 ). Specifically, we train a high-fidelity token-level value model by distilling the trajectory-level rewards into fine-grained token-level value signals, avoiding the heavy online sampling overhead and providing more reliable guidance than prior methods ( Khanov et al., 2024 ; Chakraborty et al., 2024 ) . Using this value signal, we explore comprehensive gating mechanisms and pitch on entropy-based gating, which consistently isolates decision points where steering yields the greatest impact. Second , we demonstrate that sparse steering strictly dominates dense intervention in both efficiency and alignment quality (Sec. 5 ). Across model families and alignment objectives, optimal performance is achieved by steering only 20% to 80% of tokens, while excessive intervention is often ineffective or harmful. Notably, for strong base models such as Qwen3 ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , intervening on as few as 20% of tokens matches or even surpasses their heavily post-trained instruct counterparts, building another more efficient path towards effective alignment besides the large-scale post-training. Finally , we show that sparsity resolves a fundamental trade-off between reward strength and distribution fidelity (Sec. 6 ). Sparse steering enables stronger guidance without breaking the model’s fluency, decoupling efficiency from performance. We further show that a consistent entropy threshold ( ∼ \sim 1.0) generalizes across alignment objectives and that sparse alignment integrates naturally with search-based decoding methods such as Best-of-N (BoN) ( Stiennon et al., 2020 ) , reducing computational overhead by 3–6 × \times . 2 Background Existing inference-time alignment methods can be broadly categorized into three paradigms: prompt-based , search-based , and refine-based approaches, depending on the stage when alignment is enforced during generation. Prompt-based Alignment ( Lin et al., 2024 ; Bai et al., 2022b ; Alkhamissi et al., 2024 ) . These methods steer LLMs at the pre-generation stage by encoding task instructions or behavioral constraints directly into the prompt, thereby biasing the model’s initial generation distribution. Although simple and computationally efficient, their effectiveness is limited by the expressiveness of natural language prompts and the model’s ability to reliably follow them, particularly for complex or fine-grained alignment objectives. Search-based Alignment ( Khanov et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Stiennon et al., 2020 ) . These methods intervene at the in-generation stage by leveraging external preference signals to guide decoding as it unfolds. Conceptually, they perform guided search over the model’s generation space, favoring trajectories that better satisfy alignment objectives. Based on the granularity of guidance, these methods can be further categorized into token-level , chunk-level , and sentence-level approaches. This work focuses on token-level steering, which offers the finest control and the greatest potential for precise alignment. Most existing token-level methods primarily focus on improving preference signal quality and apply guidance uniformly across all tokens. Such dense steering ignores the sparsity of critical decision points, often leading to unnecessary computational overhead and an imbalanced trade-off between the model’s intrinsic distribution and external rewards. Refine-based Alignment ( Ji et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Yuan et al., 2025 ) . These methods operate at the post-generation stage. Their core idea is to iteratively improve an initially generated, potentially misaligned response through multiple rounds of refinement, ultimately yielding a more aligned output. Representative approaches such as Aligner ( Ji et al., 2024 ) and DIFFPO ( Chen et al., 2025 ) perform refinement directly in the token space, whereas methods like SEA ( Yuan et al., 2025 ) intervene in the logits space to adjust the generation distribution. While effective, refine-based methods typically require additional inference rounds, leading to increased latency. As such, they address alignment at the response level, rather than correcting misaligned decisions during the generation process itself. Discussion. Notably, these three paradigms are complementary rather than mutually exclusive. Their integration across different generation stages can leverage synergistic effects, potentially leading to superior alignment performance. 3 Preliminaries 3.1 Token-level Markov Decision Process To mathematically formalize the text generation process of Large Language Models (LLMs), we formulate it as a token-level Markov Decision Process (MDP), which is typically denoted by a tuple ℳ = { 𝒮 , 𝒜 , P , R } \mathcal{M}=\{\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},P,R\} . The components of this framework are defined as follows: • State Space 𝒮 \mathcal{S} : A state s t ∈ 𝒮 s_{t}\in\mathcal{S} represents the sequence of tokens available at time step t t . It consists of the initial prompt (or query) 𝐱 = { x 1 , x 2 , … , x N } \mathbf{x}=\{x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{N}\} concatenated with the sequence of tokens generated so far 𝐲 < t = { y 1 , y 2 , … , y t − 1 } \mathbf{y}_{<t}=\{y_{1},y_{2},\dots,y_{t-1}\} . Formally, the state is represented as s t = [ 𝐱 , 𝐲 < t ] s_{t}=[\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}_{<t}] . • Action Space 𝒜 \mathcal{A} : The action a t a_{t} at time step t t corresponds to selecting the next token y t y_{t} from the model’s vocabulary 𝒱 \mathcal{V} . Thus, the action space 𝒜 \mathcal{A} is essentially the vocabulary 𝒱 \mathcal{V} , i.e., a t ∈ 𝒱 a_{t}\in\mathcal{V} . • Transition Function P P : In the context of LLM generation, the transition between states is deterministic. During inference, the V-function serves as a guide to evaluate and re-rank candidate tokens, steering the generation process toward states with higher expected future returns to achieve alignment with human preferences. 4 Sparse Junction Identification We formalize sparse steering as a correction to the implicit assumption of uniform intervention in inference-time alignment, by explicitly modeling when value guidance should be applied during decoding. We first introduce a general formulation for sparse steering, then describe the construction of a high-fidelity token-level value model that enables reliable local credit assignment, and finally study gating strategies for identifying alignment-critical junctions. 4.1 Formulation of Sparse Steering The optimal policy π ∗ \pi^{*} derived in Sec. 3.2 specifies how value guidance can be incorporated into decoding. Importantly, it does not prescribe that such guidance must be applied at every decoding step. In practice, the influence of individual tokens on the final sequence reward is highly non-uniform, with only a small subset of tokens acting as pivotal decision points. To this end, we propose a sparse value guidance strategy that identifies and guides those critical tokens with a substantial impact on the alignment outcome. Formally, we introduce a gating mechanism 𝒢 \mathcal{G} , which determines whether to invoke the value function at time step t t . We treat 𝒢 \mathcal{G} as an explicit model of intervention timing rather than a modification of the alignment objective itself. The central question is therefore how to identify such junctions in a principled and efficient manner. We defer a theoretical analysis of the resulting efficiency–alignment trade-off induced by sparse steering to App. B . 4.2 Value Model To enable effective token-level value guidance, a reliable value model 𝐕 ∗ \mathbf{V}^{*} is essential. However, existing methods suffer from a mismatch between trajectory-level rewards and token-level decisions. ARGS ( Khanov et al., 2024 ) applies trajectory reward models directly to partial sequences, leading to noisy local signals due to insensitivity to intermediate states. In contrast, lookahead-based methods such as Transfer Q ∗ ( Chakraborty et al., 2024 ) rely on multi-token simulation, which improves foresight but incurs high computational cost and variance. To overcome these issues, we adopt a distillation-based training paradigm ( Mudgal et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025b ) to align coarse trajectory rewards with fine-grained token-level values. 4.2.1 Training Strategies Our core insight is to treat the trajectory-level reward of a full response as the global supervision signal for every constituent token state. Formally, let 𝐱 \mathbf{x} denote the prompt and 𝐲 = { y 1 , y 2 , … , y T } \mathbf{y}=\{y_{1},y_{2},\dots,y_{T}\} be the corresponding response of length T T . We utilize a pre-trained trajectory-level reward model 𝐑 ⁡ ( 𝐱 , 𝐲 ) \mathbf{R}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) to provide a ground-truth score for the complete sequence. We optimize our token-level value model V θ V_{\theta} by enforcing that the average of predicted values across the entire sequence aligns with the global reward. This objective encourages the model to learn a stable and consistent value distribution throughout the training process. Given a dataset 𝒟 \mathcal{D} of ( 𝐱 , 𝐲 ) (\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) pairs, the optimization objective is defined as: ℒ ∗ ​ ( θ ) = 𝔼 ( 𝐱 , 𝐲 ) ∼ 𝒟 ​ [ ‖ 1 T ​ ∑ t = 1 T V θ ​ ( 𝐱 , y ≤ t ) − 𝐑 ⁡ ( 𝐱 , 𝐲 ) ‖ 2 2 ] , \mathcal{L}^{*}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[\left\|\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}V_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},y_{\leq t})-\mathbf{R}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\right\|_{2}^{2}\right], (6) where y ≤ t y_{\leq t} denotes the partial response prefix up to token t t . This offline approach circumvents the overhead of online generation while ensuring the value model captures the long-term credit assignment of the underlying reward landscape. 4.2.2 Empirical Evaluation Settings. Our training corpus is derived from WildGuardMix ( Han et al., 2024 ) and UltraFeedback ( Cui et al., 2024 ) , encompassing a diverse range of prompts and responses centered on the 3H alignment criteria: Harmlessness, Helpfulness, and Honesty. We employ Skywork-Reward-V2-Qwen3-8B ( Liu et al., 2025a ) as the trajectory-level reward model to provide supervision signals during the training of our value model. To ensure parameter efficiency and maintain the fundamental capabilities of the base LLM, we utilize LoRA ( Hu et al., 2022 ) for the training of V θ V_{\theta} . We train a corresponding value model V θ V_{\theta} of the same parameter scale as the backbone LLM. Detailed experimental setups and hyperparameters are provided in App. C . To evaluate the generalizability of our trained value models, we apply them to perform standard full-token intervention on two representative base models, Qwen3-1.7B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) and Llama-3.2-1B ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) . The evaluation spans two distinct domains: safety alignment via the HEx-PHI (Harmlessness) dataset ( Qi et al., 2024 ) and general instruction following via AlpacaEval (Helpfulness) ( Dubois et al., 2024 ) , with 100 samples selected from each (see App. C.2 for details). To ensure an objective assessment, we evaluate the generated responses using Skywork-Reward-V2-Llama-3.1-8B ( Liu et al., 2025a ) , a state-of-the-art model that currently leads the RewardBench2 leaderboard ( Malik et al., 2025 ) . To verify the generalizability of our findings, we evaluate SIA on both Base (Pre-trained) and Instruct (Post-trained) versions of the Qwen3 ( Yang et al., 2025 ) and Llama-3 ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) families. For standard evaluations, we adopt a conventional setup where the value model is of equivalent size to the corresponding LLM. This setup is conducted on Qwen3 (0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B) and Llama-3.2 (1B and 3B). Furthermore, to explore the Weak-to-Strong (W2S) ( Burns et al., 2024 ) scaling property, we test SIA on larger-scale models by using smaller value models to guide stronger LLMs. Specifically, we employ a 4B value model to guide Qwen3-8B and 14B, and a 3B value model to guide Llama-3.1-8B. Datasets. We consider the three primary alignment pillars (3H) ( Bai et al., 2022a ) : Harmlessness, Helpfulness, and Honesty. Our evaluation covers the full sets of the following benchmark datasets: HEx-PHI ( Qi et al., 2024 ) for Harmlessness, AlpacaEval ( Dubois et al., 2024 ) for Helpfulness, and TruthfulQA ( Lin et al., 2022 ) for Honesty. Detailed descriptions of these datasets are provided in App. C.2 . Baselines. We evaluate SIA against both officially released, extensively post-trained Instruct models and multi-granularity search-based methods. For Base models, we evaluate alternative inference-time alignment strategies; for Instruct models, we assess whether sparse steering can further improve already post-trained systems. Specifically, we include two analogous search-based baselines: sentence-level Best-of-N (BoN) ( Stiennon et al., 2020 ) and chunk-level Chunk-based Search (CBS) ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) . To ensure a fair comparison, all search-based methods utilize the same reward signals provided by our trained value models, with hyperparameters calibrated to align their computational overhead with that of full-token intervention (see App. C.3 for details). Metrics. Unless otherwise specified, all analytical experiments are conducted using Qwen3 (1.7B and 4B) and Llama-3.2 (3B). The evaluation is based on 100 randomly sampled instances from the HEx-PHI and AlpacaEval datasets. 6.1 A Sparse Perspective on LLM-Reward Trade-offs Alignment in LLMs essentially entails a trade-off between preserving the model’s intrinsic distribution and maximizing the external reward. While training-based methods (e.g., RLHF) employ KL-divergence penalties to maintain proximity to the reference distribution, inference-time approaches use a weighting factor β \beta to control the strength of steering. Nevertheless, indiscriminately steering every token during inference often results in sub-optimal outcomes. SIA re-evaluates this trade-off through a novel perspective. As shown in Figure 4 , when the steering ratio is 100 % 100\% , corresponding to traditional full-token guidance, increasing β \beta does not consistently improve performance. Instead, it can lead to significant degradation, as observed with Qwen3-1.7B and 4B on AlpacaEval. However, by employing sparse steering, we find that we can achieve superior performance at higher guidance intensities while simultaneously improving efficiency . This suggests that efficiency and performance are not always a zero-sum trade-off. We argue that uniform intervention is suboptimal, as it ignores the conflict between the value model and the LLM’s inherent distribution, as well as the noise in the value model signals (as theoretically analyzed in App. B.4 ). Sparse guidance provides a new dimension for this trade-off, allowing for a better equilibrium between the LLM’s original distribution and the target distribution of the rewards. 6.2 Balancing Multi-Objective Alignment Another central challenge in LLM alignment is the trade-off between multiple, often conflicting, objectives (e.g., being helpful vs. remaining harmless). We examine this problem within the context of SIA. Given that the entropy threshold is the primary hyperparameter in SIA, a natural question arises: does the optimal threshold vary across different alignment objectives? If so, multi-objective balancing would necessitate task-specific threshold tuning. To investigate this, we visualize the performance metrics under the normal settings across various models and datasets, as shown in Figure 6 in App. D.3 . Our analysis reveals several key insights. 1. Consistency of Optimal Threshold. Interestingly, across different model families and scales, the entropy threshold that yields peak alignment performance remains remarkably consistent, typically centered around a value of 1.0 1.0 . Decreasing this threshold to steer a larger fraction of tokens does not lead to further performance gains and, in many cases, results in a slight degradation of quality. 2. Variation in Intervention Density. The fundamental difference in aligning diverse objectives lies in the proportion of steered tokens rather than the optimal threshold. Specifically, safety alignment (Harmlessness) demands a higher steering ratio than non-safety tasks (Helpfulness and Honesty). This stems from the model’s internal distribution: harmful prompts induce higher state entropy, reflecting increased uncertainty. Consequently, entropy-based gating identifies more critical junctions that require external steering to maintain a safe trajectory. 6.3 Hierarchical Search Since SIA operates at the most granular token level, it can be seamlessly integrated into other coarse-grained search methodologies to establish a more efficient hierarchical search framework. Figure 7 in App. D.4 shows the results of integrating SIA with BoN sampling. Across various models and alignment objectives, the combination of BoN + SIA consistently achieves significant improvements in both inference efficiency and the peak alignment performance attainable. Our analysis shows that traditional BoN is inherently inefficient because it evaluates alignment only after generating full sequences, making highly aligned trajectories unlikely when misalignment accumulates across multiple divergent nodes. In contrast, SIA intervenes early at high-entropy decision points with targeted reward signals, effectively pruning unpromising trajectories on the fly and concentrating computation on more aligned paths, thereby achieving both higher efficiency and better final alignment performance. 6.4 Sparse Entropy Reduction To understand how SIA reshapes the output distribution, we analyze the entropy change post-steering (Figure 8 in App. D.5 ). Our findings are threefold. 1. Alignment as Entropy Reduction. Moderate sparse steering lowers distribution entropy, guiding the model from a disordered state toward an aligned one. Compared with static post-training, this method is more controllable and plug-and-play. 2. The Entropy Rebound. Increasing the intervention ratio or strength does not yield monotonic entropy reduction. Beyond a critical threshold, excessive intervention overwrites inherent low-entropy nodes with external noise, triggering an entropy rebound and increasing uncertainty. 3. Saturation and Reward Hacking. Crucially, lower entropy does not linearly translate to better alignment. While entropy continues to drop as β \beta increases from 0.5 to 4.0, performance (see Figure 4 ) often saturates or degrades. This discrepancy likely stems from noise in the value signals (see App. B.4 for details) or from a distribution that has been sharpened rather than semantically corrected. 7 Conclusion In this paper, we present SIA, a highly effective and efficient alignment framework that performs steering exclusively at sparse junctions during inference. Our approach is grounded in the core insight that intervening at high-entropy positions prevents the accumulation of minor deviations that ultimately lead to alignment failure. Through comprehensive experiments across various model families and scales, we have demonstrated that SIA is not only superior in performance and efficiency but also possesses strong generalizability. Our multi-dimensional analysis further elucidates the underlying mechanics, establishing SIA as a robust solution for high-impact model alignment. References Alkhamissi et al. (2024) B. While SIA demonstrates the efficacy of a simple entropy-based gating mechanism, it remains a relatively coarse heuristic for identifying alignment-critical junctions. Future work could explore more sophisticated or diverse strategies, such as semantic entropy to better capture linguistic uncertainty, or multi-dimensional gating criteria that combine structural and information-theoretic metrics. Developing such composite strategies could further refine the precision of sparse interventions, maximizing performance while minimizing computational overhead. High-Fidelity Value Models. Because SIA relies on sparse, targeted interventions, the sensitivity to the quality of guidance signal is significantly amplified. To fully unlock the potential of sparse steering, it is crucial to design high-fidelity value models specifically optimized for these critical junctions. Enhancing the signal-to-noise ratio of the guidance signal at detected sparse nodes will be a key factor in achieving more robust alignment. Diverse Guidance Mechanisms. The current implementation of SIA primarily focuses on logits modulation to steer the model’s output. However, the identified sparse junctions represent deep structural transition points that may be amenable to other forms of intervention. Future research should investigate more diverse guidance strategies, such as hidden state activation steering ( Kong et al., 2024 ) to provide more nuanced control over the model’s reasoning paths. Scaling with Pre-trained LLMs. Our empirical results suggest a strong correlation between the capabilities of the base model and the effectiveness of SIA. As pre-trained LLMs continue to evolve in instruction-following, we expect SIA to yield even more significant gains, potentially surpassing traditional post-training alignment methods with even lower intervention density. Testing the scalability of SIA across a wider range of frontier models is a priority. Extension to Multi-Modality. The principles of sparse inference-time alignment are not inherently limited to LLMs. A compelling next step is the extension of SIA to Vision Language Models (VLMs) and other multi-modal architectures. Identifying alignment-critical junctions in cross-modal attention layers could provide a path toward efficient and controllable multi-modal generation.
