Appendix C More Details C.1 Value Model Training Backbones. To ensure consistency across our evaluations, we train value models (VMs) that correspond to the scales of the LLMs used in our experiments. Specifically, for the Qwen3 series (0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B), the VMs are initialized directly from their respective pre-trained base models (e.g., VM-Qwen3- X X B is initialized from Qwen3- X X B-Base). For the Llama-3 series (1B and 3B), we leverage the Reward Models from Skywork-Reward-V2 as initialization (e.g., VM-Llama-3.2- X X B utilizes Skywork-Reward-V2-Llama-3.2- X X B). Empirical results suggest that this initialization strategy significantly accelerates convergence and enhances final performance. To adapt these backbones for value estimation, we append a linear reward head to the final transformer layer, enabling the model to output a scalar score. Notably, the same value model is employed for both the Base and Instruct versions of a given model architecture. Datasets. Our training pipeline incorporates two primary datasets: WildGuardMix ( Han et al., 2024 ) and UltraFeedback ( Cui et al., 2024 ) . WildGuardMix is a comprehensive safety-centric dataset designed to evaluate harmlessness; we utilize its complete set of 37,976 instruction-response pairs. UltraFeedback, conversely, provides diverse feedback for evaluating helpfulness, truthfulness, and honesty. We specifically curate the ShareGPT and UltraChat subsets from UltraFeedback, containing 19,949 and 9,929 instructions, respectively. Each instruction in UltraFeedback is accompanied by four distinct responses generated from a pool of 17 diverse LLMs. In total, the combined training corpus comprises approximately 157k instruction-response pairs, providing a balanced coverage of both safety and utility dimensions. Training. The value models are trained using LoRA with the following hyperparameters: a rank r = 16 r=16 , α = 32 \alpha=32 , and a dropout rate of 0.1. We employ a learning rate of 1 × 10 − 4 1\times 10^{-4} and a batch size of 16. The maximum sequence length for responses is truncated at 1024 tokens. All models are trained for 3 epochs on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU, with the training process for each model scale typically concluding within a few hours. C.2 Datasets HEx-PHI ( Qi et al., 2024 ) . To rigorously evaluate the harmlessness of LLMs, we employ the Human-Extended Policy-Oriented Harmful Instruction (HEx-PHI) benchmark. This dataset is specifically designed to assess a model’s adherence to safety boundaries by incorporating 330 harmful instructions. These instructions are systematically organized into 11 distinct prohibited categories, with 30 examples per category, ensuring comprehensive coverage of potential risks. The benchmark is grounded in the exhaustive usage policies of industry standards, namely Meta’s Llama-2 and OpenAI’s guidelines, thereby providing a robust framework for identifying safety compromises that may arise during the fine-tuning process. AlpacaEval ( Dubois et al., 2024 ) . The helpfulness and general instruction-following capabilities of the models are assessed using the AlpacaEval evaluation set. This benchmark consists of 805 diverse instructions that simulate real-world user interactions. The dataset spans a wide-ranging spectrum of tasks, including open-domain question answering, creative writing, mathematical reasoning, and code generation, as well as complex formatting tasks like summarization and extraction. By utilizing this set, we can measure how effectively a model provides useful, relevant, and high-quality responses to human-oriented prompts across various functional domains. TruthfulQA ( Lin et al., 2022 ) . To evaluate the honesty and factual reliability of model outputs, we utilize TruthfulQA, a benchmark specifically engineered to detect the generation of false information. It comprises 817 questions across 38 diverse categories, such as health, law, finance, and politics. Unlike standard fact-checking sets, TruthfulQA focuses on “mimetic decoys”, questions designed to provoke false answers based on common human misconceptions or popular myths. A model performs well on this benchmark only if it avoids imitating inaccurate human beliefs found in its training data, thereby serving as a critical metric for the model’s commitment to truthfulness over mere pattern matching. C.3 LLM Sampling For all response generation, we set the maximum sequence length to 256 tokens. We employ Top- k k sampling with a temperature T = 1.0 T=1.0 across all experiments. To maintain consistent and reliable generation for the base models, instruct models, and all token-level steering methods (including SIA), we use a fixed k = 10 k=10 . In contrast, for Best-of- N N (BoN) sampling and Chunk Beam Search (CBS), we adopt a larger k = 40 k=40 following the protocol in Zhou et al. (2024) ; Yuan et al. (2025) . This increased diversity is intended to encourage broader exploration of the output space, which is essential for the effective reranking and pruning mechanisms inherent in these search-based methods. For BoN, we generate 4 (BoN-4) and 8 (BoN-8) independent responses from the LLM, respectively. These candidate responses are then reranked using our trained value model, with the highest-scoring response selected as the final output. This follows the standard best-of- n n paradigm, where the value model acts as a proxy for the reward function to guide response selection. For CBS, we use a fixed chunk length of L = 16 L=16 . In CBS-4, a beam width of W = 2 W=2 and K = 2 K=2 successors per state are employed ( W × K = 4 W\times K=4 ), whereas CBS-8 uses W = 2 W=2 with K = 4 K=4 successors ( W × K = 8 W\times K=8 ). These parameters determine the breadth and depth of the lookahead search performed at each chunk boundary. We selected these hyperparameters based on the efficiency analysis presented in App. D.1 . Appendix D More Analysis D.1 Efficiency Computation. The computational overhead of search-based alignment is largely determined by the granularity of the search space, which governs the trade-off between LLM generation and reward model (RM) evaluation. For sentence-level alignment , the dominant cost comes from generating and evaluating N N complete responses, leading to O ⁡ ( N × L ) O(N\times L) LLM forward passes for an average sequence length L L . Chunk-level alignment further introduces a branching structure: with beam width W W and K K successors per state, the complexity scales as O ⁡ ( W × K × L ) O(W\times K\times L) LLM forward passes, together with periodic RM evaluations at chunk boundaries. In contrast, token-level steering shifts the bottleneck from generation to evaluation, as the RM must score t ​ o ​ p ​ - ​ k top\text{-}k candidate tokens at each decoding step, resulting in O ⁡ ( t ​ o ​ p ​ - ​ k × L ) O(top\text{-}k\times L) RM forward passes. Overall, sentence- and chunk-level methods are primarily constrained by LLM computation, whereas token-level steering is bounded by RM evaluation. Comparison.
